Before? No, not really in the way you mean. I mean, people make remarks, people are careless, there’s always office chatter or some neighbor saying something in the hallway. I didn’t used to sit there thinking it was about me.

This apartment is different. That’s the point I keep trying to explain. And they show me paperwork, give explanations, say it’s maintenance or mix-ups, but paperwork doesn’t erase what’s happening. Before this place, no, I wouldn’t say ordinary things felt directed at me like that. Here, they are.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Clear proof is a strong phrase. People wave paperwork around and call it proof all the time. I worked with documents for years—reports, memos, charts—and I can tell you, a neat explanation doesn’t necessarily mean it’s the real explanation.

If someone could truly show me, I mean truly show me, that all the misdelivered mail and the noises in the walls and the little neighbor comments were just ordinary building issues… I’d look at it. I’m not unreasonable. But that’s not what’s been happening. For months, the timing and the pattern have been too consistent. They keep saying “maintenance” or “mistake,” and somehow it always lines up in a way that pressures me.

So I don’t think a stack of papers from the property manager would change what I can see. That’s part of the problem—they think if they make it look official, I’ll stop noticing.

I used to deal with reports where you had to allow for error, missing data, all of that. But this isn’t one isolated thing I’m overreacting to.\n\nFor months it’s been the mail going to the wrong place, then noises in the walls at very specific times, then neighbors making these little comments that sound casual if you repeat them later but fit exactly with what’s been happening. And the property manager gives paperwork or explanations like that settles it, but it doesn’t. The pattern is still there.\n\nSo no, I don’t really think I’m mistaken about them trying to pressure me out. That’s what’s happening.\n\nDoctor: Has anything happened that makes you think someone can affect you through the walls in a way that would normally seem impossible?\n\nPatient: I wouldn’t put it like “impossible,” no. That makes it sound like I’m saying something out of a movie, and I’m not.\n\nWhat I’m saying is the noises in the walls happen at very specific times, along with the mail being “misdelivered” and neighbors making these little comments that line up too neatly. It’s the pattern. I used to spend my whole career looking at patterns in information, and when people hand you paperwork saying, “Oh, this was just a mistake,” that doesn’t erase what’s actually happening.\n\nSo through the walls? It’s the timed noises, yes. But I’m not saying magic or anything like that. I’m saying they’re using the building, the walls, the little disturbances, to pressure me out.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard a voice speaking when no one was actually there?\n\nPatient: A voice? I’m more concerned with the timing of things and how they line up, not voices out of nowhere.\n\nDoctor: Aside from the situation in your building, have you had any trouble keeping up with your usual daily activities?\n\nPatient: No, not really. I don’t know about that. I mean, people can guess things, can’t they? I haven’t really noticed that. Sometimes someone will say something that lines up too neatly with what I was just thinking, but that happens. Or maybe you remember it because it’s odd. Complete certainty… I mean, that’s a phrase lawyers like, isn’t it? “Complete certainty.” In my old job, we were careful with words like that because people could twist a conclusion depending on what column they put the numbers in.

I’m here because for months the property manager and certain people in the building have been doing these things—mail going to the wrong place, noises in the walls at just the right times, little comments from neighbors that seem casual if you take them one by one. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Before this apartment situation? I’m trying to think what you mean exactly—like seeing a person standing there who wasn’t there, or hearing a voice? No, I don’t think so. Not that anyone ever pointed out to me.

I’ve always been observant, maybe more than some people. In an office, especially doing analysis, you learn to notice small discrepancies—sounds in the hallway, who said what in a meeting, numbers that changed from one version to the next. People act like noticing things is strange when it’s inconvenient for them.

But before all this with the apartment… no, I can’t recall anything like what you’re describing.

But this isn’t one isolated thing I’m overreacting to.\n\nFor months it’s been the mail going to the wrong place, then noises in the walls at very specific times, then neighbors making these little comments that sound casual if you repeat them later but fit exactly with what’s been happening. And the property manager gives paperwork or explanations like that settles it, but it doesn’t. The pattern is still there.\n\nSo no, I don’t really think I’m mistaken about them trying to pressure me out. That’s what’s happening.\n\nDoctor: Has anything happened that makes you think someone can affect you through the walls in a way that would normally seem impossible?\n\nPatient: I wouldn’t put it like “impossible,” no. That makes it sound like I’m saying something out of a movie, and I’m not.\n\nWhat I’m saying is the noises in the walls happen at very specific times, along with the mail being “misdelivered” and neighbors making these little comments that line up too neatly. It’s the pattern. I used to spend my whole career looking at patterns in information, and when people hand you paperwork saying, “Oh, this was just a mistake,” that doesn’t erase what’s actually happening.\n\nSo through the walls? It’s the timed noises, yes. But I’m not saying magic or anything like that. I’m saying they’re using the building, the walls, the little disturbances, to pressure me out.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard a voice speaking when no one was actually there?\n\nPatient: A voice? No, I don’t—well, I don’t think that’s the right way to put it. I hear people in the hall sometimes, or noises through the walls, but that’s an apartment building, and sound carries. It’s an old building, too, you know, the kind where you can hear plumbing and footsteps and all that.\n\nBut a voice speaking when no one’s there… I haven’t noticed that, no. I’m more concerned with the timing of things and how they line up, not voices out of nowhere.\n\nDoctor: Aside from the situation in your building, have you had any trouble keeping up with your usual daily activities?\n\nPatient: No, not really. I mean, if I’m not having to deal with all the apartment nonsense, I can keep up with things. I pay my bills, I manage my accounts, I cook for myself. I still get to appointments.\n\nAnd I can talk perfectly clearly about work-type things, consulting, analysis, that kind of thing. Or painting, actually—I’ve been doing more of that. Years ago I had this whole system for organizing color studies, which sounds unrelated, but it’s the same part of my mind, you know, keeping things ordered.\n\nSo day to day, yes, I manage. It’s just when the building situation intrudes that it takes up a lot of my attention.\n\nDoctor: About how long has this been going on?\n\nPatient: About eleven months, I think. It started not long after I moved into that apartment.\n\nAt first I thought, well, new building, new routines, you notice things more. When I was working, moving offices was like that too—everyone says the copier noise is “normal” until you realize it’s always at the same time. But yes, if you want the straight answer, it’s been roughly eleven months.\n\nDoctor: Have you had the sense that other people can know your thoughts, even when you haven’t said them out loud?\n\nPatient: Know my thoughts? I don’t know about that. I mean, people can guess things, can’t they? Especially if you’ve worked with people for years—meetings, evaluations, all those little expressions people make before they’ve even said what they mean.\n\nBut thoughts, like directly? I haven’t really noticed that. Sometimes someone will say something that lines up too neatly with what I was just thinking, but that happens. Or maybe you remember it because it’s odd. So… no, I’m not sure I’d put it that way.\n\nDoctor: Before you moved into this apartment, did you generally tend to distrust other people and suspect they had hidden motives?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I’ve always been careful with people, I suppose—when you work in management analysis, you learn people don’t always say the real reason for a decision. There’s the official reason, and then there’s the budget reason, or the political reason, or someone protecting their department.\n\nBut distrust everyone? No, I don’t think I walked around assuming that. I had colleagues I trusted, neighbors I’d nod to, people at the grocery store—ordinary things. Hidden motives... I mean, everyone has motives, don’t they? That doesn’t mean I thought they were all out to do something. Before the apartment, I don’t think it occupied me like this.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed yourself becoming much less emotionally expressive or less motivated than you used to be?\n\nPatient: Less emotionally expressive? I don’t know. I’ve never been someone who throws his arms around or makes a big performance of feelings. In my line of work, you learn to keep a neutral face in meetings—otherwise people read things into it. One raised eyebrow and suddenly it’s “he’s against the proposal,” when really you’re just thinking about whether the numbers add up.\n\nMotivation… I mean, I still do what needs doing, more or less. Some days I don’t feel like starting things, but I’m 65, not 25. I don’t know if that’s motivation or just being tired of nonsense. So no, I haven’t really noticed a big change like that.\n\nDoctor: Before this apartment situation began, did you often feel that ordinary remarks or events were directed specifically at you or carried a special meaning for you?\n\nPatient: Before? No, not really in the way you mean. I mean, people make remarks, people are careless, there’s always office chatter or some neighbor saying something in the hallway. I didn’t used to sit there thinking it was about me.\n\nThis apartment is different. That’s the point I keep trying to explain. For months now it’s been the property manager and certain people in the building—mail ending up “accidentally” misdelivered, noises in the walls right when I’m doing something, little comments from neighbors that sound innocent if you take them one at a time. But together, there’s a pattern. They’re trying to pressure me out.\n\nAnd they show me paperwork, give explanations, say it’s maintenance or mix-ups, but paperwork doesn’t erase what’s happening. Before this place, no, I wouldn’t say ordinary things felt directed at me like that. Here, they are.\n\nDoctor: If someone showed you clear proof that the mail problems and noises were ordinary building issues, would you be able to accept that?\n\nPatient: Clear proof is a strong phrase. People wave paperwork around and call it proof all the time. I worked with documents for years—reports, memos, charts—and I can tell you, a neat explanation doesn’t necessarily mean it’s the real explanation.\n\nIf someone could truly show me, I mean truly show me, that all the misdelivered mail and the noises in the walls and the little neighbor comments were just ordinary building issues… I’d look at it. I’m not unreasonable. But that’s not what’s been happening. For months, the timing and the pattern have been too consistent. They keep saying “maintenance” or “mistake,” and somehow it always lines up in a way that pressures me.\n\nSo I don’t think a stack of papers from the property manager would change what I can see. That’s part of the problem—they think if they make it look official, I’ll stop noticing.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt that your thoughts or actions were being controlled by some outside force?\n\nPatient: Controlled? No, not like a machine or something, if that’s what you mean. I decide what I do.\n\nBut I do think they’re trying to push me, pressure me—there’s a difference. The property manager, and a few people in the building, they’ve been doing this for months. The mail gets “misdelivered,” noises start up in the walls at very particular times, neighbors make these little comments that sound harmless unless you’ve been living with the whole pattern. It’s like they want me unsettled enough to leave.\n\nAnd they can bring out paperwork, explanations, maintenance notices—fine, I used to deal with documents for a living, so I know how official something can look without telling the whole story. That doesn’t mean they’re controlling my thoughts or actions. It means they’re trying to pressure me out of my apartment, and I can see it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized and needed much less sleep than usual?\n\nPatient: Unusually energized… I don’t know. Management analysis isn’t exactly glamorous, but if numbers don’t line up, you don’t just go to bed and pretend they do. You keep at it.\n\nSo… no, I can’t say I’ve noticed some special period like that. Not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe with complete certainty that the people in your building are deliberately trying to force you out?\n\nPatient: Complete certainty… I mean, that’s a phrase lawyers like, isn’t it? “Complete certainty.” In my old job, we were careful with words like that because people could twist a conclusion depending on what column they put the numbers in.\n\nBut yes, I know what I’ve been seeing. I’m here because for months the property manager and certain people in the building have been doing these things—mail going to the wrong place, noises in the walls at just the right times, little comments from neighbors that seem casual if you take them one by one. But when you put them together, there’s a pattern. And it’s not accidental.\n\nThey want me pressured enough to leave the apartment. That’s what it comes down to. They can call it maintenance, they can show me notices or paperwork, but paperwork doesn’t erase a pattern you’re living inside every day.\n\nDoctor: Have other people told you that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another?\n\nPatient: Hard to follow? I don’t know. People say that when they don’t want to follow, sometimes.\n\nI mean, I’ve always explained things with context. In my old work, if you just gave the conclusion without the supporting pieces, someone would say you hadn’t justified it. So I might circle around a bit, yes, but that’s because details matter. One thing connects to another—otherwise people pretend it’s all separate.\n\nNo one’s sat me down and said, “Your speech is impossible to follow,” not that I remember. Maybe they get impatient. That’s different.\n\nDoctor: Before this apartment situation started, had you ever heard or seen things that other people said weren’t there?\n\nPatient: Before this apartment situation? I’m trying to think what you mean exactly—like seeing a person standing there who wasn’t there, or hearing a voice? No, I don’t think so. Not that anyone ever pointed out to me.\n\nI’ve always been observant, maybe more than some people. In an office, especially doing analysis, you learn to notice small discrepancies—sounds in the hallway, who said what in a meeting, numbers that changed from one version to the next. People act like noticing things is strange when it’s inconvenient for them.\n\nBut before all this with the apartment… no, I can’t recall anything like what you’re describing.\n\nDoctor: Outside of the situation in your apartment building, have you felt that things like television, radio, or newspapers were sending messages meant specifically for you?\n\nPatient: Television or newspapers… no, that’s not really the issue. Put together, it’s pressure. They want me out of the apartment. Their notices and explanations don’t change what I’m seeing."
